title: Project to boost Trans Mountain pipeline flows starts up ahead of schedule
html:
Tankers are docked at the Trans Mountain Westridge Marine Terminal, where crude oil from the expanded Trans Mountain Pipeline is loaded onto tankers, in Burnaby, B.C., in 2024.DARRYL DYCK/The Canadian Press

A project to increase the amount of crude that can flow on the Trans Mountain Pipeline using chemical additives has been completed two months ahead of schedule, the Crown corporation said as it released third-quarter results on Friday.

The drag-reducing agent increases the pipeline’s capacity by up to about 10 per cent to 980,000 barrels per day. Trans Mountain carries oil from the Edmonton area to Burnaby, B.C.

“We started moving more volume in October and basically are full here in November and expect to be full in December,” Trans Mountain CEO Mark Maki said in an interview.

When Trans Mountain sought bids from customers this summer to ship more of their oil on the line, demand was 5½ times what was being offered.

A further expansion of 210,000 barrels per day, using new pipeline segments and pump stations, is expected to come into service by the end of 2028, bringing the system’s total capacity to 1.19 million barrels a day.

During the third quarter, Trans Mountain shipped 840,000 barrels per day on average, up from 777,000 barrels during the same three months of 2025. About 60 per cent of the throughput during the period went to the Westridge Marine Terminal, with most of the oil-laden tankers sailing across the Pacific to Asian customers, Maki said. The rest went to delivery points in B.C. and Washington State via pipeline.

Net income for the quarter rose to $132-million from $127-million as revenues increased to $825-million from $765-million.

So far this year, Trans Mountain has paid $1.45-billion to its owner, the federal government, in interest payments, dividends and return of capital distributions. For the quarter, a total of $551-million went to Ottawa.

Ottawa bought the pipeline for $4.5-billion in 2018 after Kinder Morgan Canada walked away from a project to triple the line’s capacity at the time, amid fierce environmental opposition and court challenges. It ended up costing more than $34-billion by the time the expanded pipeline started up in May of 2024.

Federal and Trans Mountain officials have said there is no rush to return the pipeline to the private sector. Some Indigenous groups have long expressed interest taking a stake in the pipeline.

Trans Mountain said in its Friday news release that confidential information sessions with potential Indigenous partners began in October. Meetings have been held in Edmonton, Kamloops, Victoria and Vancouver and were well attended, Maki said.

As for when a deal might be announced, “it’ll take a while,” he added.

“There’s lots of nations and lots of considerations that they have to think through.”

Meanwhile, Trans Mountain is taking the lead on the development of the Pacific Link pipeline, a new million-barrel-a-day oil pipeline proposed by the Alberta government that would largely follow the same path as Trans Mountain, ending at a port in Delta, B.C.

Pacific Link has been designated a project of national interest, meaning it’s being guided through a streamlined regulatory process under the federal major projects office.

Before the major projects office was set up last year, a regulatory application for a project the scale of the Trans Mountain expansion completed a few years ago would have been gargantuan – filling binders lining the entire length of a boardroom table, Maki said.

“What I expect the application for the next project to be is much skinnier, so it’s changed a lot,” he said.

The changes to the process have been welcomed among those working on new projects under the new regime, but it has taken a “mindset shift,” Maki added.

“Perfection was probably the aiming point for that first filing. Here, the expectation is, it’s got to be good. And then there’ll be the expectation of some updating, refinements, changes which are effectively in process.”

At least 17 First Nations in Alberta and B.C., one U.S. tribe in Washington State and one individual have filed legal challenges against Pacific Link’s national interest designation, according to a news release Thursday distributed by the St’at’imc Chiefs Council. The St’at’imc Nation and T’Sou-ke First Nation earlier this month filed a joint application to quash Ottawa’s decision on the pipeline proposal.

In an interview earlier this week, federal Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said the major projects office and Canada Energy Regulator will be holding comprehensive consultations on the project.

“I am confident we will find a path forward,” he said. “Will there be hiccups and bumps along the way? Sure, maybe. But I am confident that we can find a win-win by working together.”

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated the total daily capacity of the Trans Mountain pipeline with its upcoming expansion. It is 1.19 million barrels.
summary: New chemical additives increase pipeline’s capacity by about 10%
